title: Cost Optimization & Architecture
subtitle: AWS Well-Architected framework, cost control strategies, and the architecture patterns that power real production systems

content.text: AWS has documented the principles behind every well-built system on their platform in the Well-Architected Framework — six pillars that every production system should be evaluated against. These aren't aspirational guidelines; they're the difference between an architecture that handles incidents gracefully and one that causes them.

content.code:
1. OPERATIONAL EXCELLENCE
   - Infrastructure as Code (CloudFormation/CDK)
   - Deploy frequently in small increments
   - Automate runbooks — no manual steps in incident response
   - Learn from every incident

2. SECURITY
   - Implement a strong identity foundation (IAM least privilege)
   - Enable traceability (CloudTrail, CloudWatch Logs)
   - Automate security best practices
   - Protect data in transit (TLS) and at rest (encryption)

3. RELIABILITY
   - Design for failure: assume components will fail
   - Multi-AZ deployments for stateful resources
   - Automatic recovery: health checks + auto-scaling
   - Test recovery procedures (game days, chaos engineering)

4. PERFORMANCE EFFICIENCY
   - Right-size resources (don't over-provision)
   - Use managed services (RDS > self-managed Postgres)
   - Experiment: test new instance types, compare costs
   - Use CDN for static assets (CloudFront)

5. COST OPTIMIZATION
   - Adopt a consumption model (pay for what you use)
   - Use Spot for interruptible workloads
   - Reserved/Savings Plans for baseline steady-state
   - Delete unused resources (biggest hidden cost)

6. SUSTAINABILITY
   - Use managed services (more efficient than self-managed)
   - Right-size resources to minimize waste
   - Use graviton instances (more efficient per compute unit)

IMMEDIATE WINS (do these first):
  1. Delete unattached EBS volumes
     aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available

  2. Delete unused Elastic IPs
     aws ec2 describe-addresses  (costs $0.005/hour if not attached)

  3. Delete old EBS snapshots, unused AMIs

  4. Stop non-production instances outside business hours
     (Lambda to stop EC2 at 6pm, start at 8am = 65% savings)

  5. Set S3 lifecycle rules for old data

RESERVED INSTANCES / SAVINGS PLANS:
  On-demand:   $0.042/hour for t3.medium
  1-year RI:   $0.026/hour for t3.medium (38% saving)
  3-year RI:   $0.016/hour for t3.medium (62% saving)
  Rule: if it runs 24/7 for > 1 year, buy Reserved Instances

SPOT INSTANCES:
  Up to 90% cheaper than on-demand
  Can be interrupted with 2-minute notice
  Use for: batch jobs, CI/CD runners, ML training, rendering
  Don't use for: stateful databases, customer-facing APIs (without graceful handling)

GRAVITON INSTANCES:
  t4g vs t3: ~20% cheaper, same performance
  m7g vs m6i: ~15% cheaper, ~20% better performance
  Requires: Linux OS, compiled-for-ARM binaries
  Docker images: add 'linux/arm64' to your multi-platform build

RIGHT-SIZING:
  Use CloudWatch metrics: if CPU < 20% average, downsize
  AWS Compute Optimizer provides recommendations automatically
  Check weekly: 'are we paying for capacity we're not using?'

content.filename: Budget alerts — never get a surprise bill
content.code:
# Create a monthly budget with email alert at 80% and 100%
aws budgets create-budget \
  --account-id $(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text) \
  --budget '{
    "BudgetName": "Monthly-Budget",
    "BudgetLimit": {"Amount": "50", "Unit": "USD"},
    "TimeUnit": "MONTHLY",
    "BudgetType": "COST"
  }' \
  --notifications-with-subscribers '[{
    "Notification": {
      "NotificationType": "ACTUAL",
      "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN",
      "Threshold": 80,
      "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"
    },
    "Subscribers": [{
      "SubscriptionType": "EMAIL",
      "Address": "alerts@mycompany.com"
    }]
  }]'

# Also enable: Billing → Preferences → Receive Billing Alerts
# Then create CloudWatch alarm on 'EstimatedCharges' metric
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name 'Monthly-Bill-Over-50' \
  --namespace AWS/Billing \
  --metric-name EstimatedCharges \
  --dimensions Name=Currency,Value=USD \
  --statistic Maximum \
  --period 86400 \
  --threshold 50 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 1 \
  --region us-east-1   # billing metrics are always in us-east-1

questions.question: Your batch processing jobs run for 6 hours every night and can restart from a checkpoint if interrupted. Which pricing model maximizes savings?
options: Spot Instances — up to 90% savings, acceptable for interruptible batch jobs
Dedicated Hosts — best for compliance workloads
questions.explanation: Spot Instances are ideal here: the jobs are interruptible (they can checkpoint and restart), they run on a schedule (not customer-facing), and the savings are massive (up to 90%). Reserved Instances give ~38-62% savings but require a 1-3 year commitment, and the batch nature (only running at night) means you'd be paying for capacity even when not using it. On-demand is the most expensive. Dedicated Hosts are for compliance, not cost savings.

faq.q: My AWS bill is too high. How do I find what's costing money?
faq.a: Use Cost Explorer (Billing → Cost Explorer) to break down costs by service, region, and resource. Sort by 'Service' to find the biggest line items. Enable Cost Allocation Tags to track costs per project/team/environment. Use 'Trusted Advisor' for automated recommendations. The most common surprise costs: forgotten EC2 instances, unattached EBS volumes, NAT Gateway data transfer, and unused Elastic IPs.

examples: Dropbox saved $75 million over 2 years by moving their primary storage infrastructure off AWS S3 to their own hardware — but they kept everything else on AWS. Right-sizing means knowing when managed cloud services are not the most cost-efficient option at scale

Netflix spent $1 billion/year on AWS at their peak. They negotiated custom Reserved Instance pricing and used Spot for batch encoding — their cloud bill at that scale was still cheaper than building and managing their own global CDN infrastructure
